title: Autumn, in Two Orbits
subtitle: Six poets. Six pauses. A season held in words and light.
authorship: Selection, commentary, interface and guided prose authored by the primary assistant; no local language model used for writing.

poems.title: To Autumn
poems.author: John Keats
poems.poem:
Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness,
  Close bosom-friend of the maturing sun;
Conspiring with him how to load and bless
  With fruit the vines that round the thatch-eves run;
To bend with apples the moss’d cottage-trees,
  And fill all fruit with ripeness to the core;
    To swell the gourd, and plump the hazel shells
  With a sweet kernel; to set budding more,
And still more, later flowers for the bees,
Until they think warm days will never cease,
    For summer has o’er-brimm’d their clammy cells.

Who hath not seen thee oft amid thy store?
  Sometimes whoever seeks abroad may find
Thee sitting careless on a granary floor,
  Thy hair soft-lifted by the winnowing wind;
Or on a half-reap’d furrow sound asleep,
  Drowsed with the fume of poppies, while thy hook
    Spares the next swath and all its twined flowers:
And sometimes like a gleaner thou dost keep
  Steady thy laden head across a brook;
  Or by a cider-press, with patient look,
    Thou watchest the last oozings, hours by hours.

Where are the songs of Spring? Ay, where are they?
  Think not of them, thou hast thy music too,—
While barred clouds bloom the soft-dying day,
  And touch the stubble-plains with rosy hue;
Then in a wailful choir the small gnats mourn
  Among the river sallows, borne aloft
    Or sinking as the light wind lives or dies;
And full-grown lambs loud bleat from hilly bourn;
  Hedge-crickets sing; and now with treble soft
  The redbreast whistles from a garden-croft,
    And gathering swallows twitter in the skies.
poems.edition: Text as presented by the Academy of American Poets; written September 19, 1819, first published 1820. Three stanzas of eleven lines.
poems.history: Keats wrote this ode on September 19, 1819; it appeared in 1820. Its three stanzas let autumn become abundance, a person resting amid harvest work, and finally a world of sound. The tools and tasks matter: winnowing separates grain from chaff, a gleaner gathers what harvesting leaves behind, and a cider press extracts apple juice. The ease of the verse includes a landscape shaped by labor.
poems.reading: The poem offers a way of attending to an ending without rushing past what remains. Its first stanza keeps adding ripeness; the second slows almost to stillness; the third makes room for smaller voices. Reading its last stanza as acceptance is one interpretation, not a statement that every autumn landscape—or every reader—must feel peaceful.
poems.detail: Read the verbs in order: load, bless, bend, fill, swell, plump. Their accumulation makes the first stanza feel full. Later, “hours by hours” lengthens the wait at the press. At the close, look away from the fruit and listen. The season acquires music instead of an answer to the question about spring.
poems.question: How much of this apparent stillness depends on keeping harvest labor at a distance?
poems.investigation: Compare the figures of the reaper and gleaner with the opening abundance. Then consult contemporary accounts of agricultural work around Winchester. The poem establishes its images; this orb does not establish the workers’ lived conditions from those images alone.
poems.feel: You may settle into a comfortable position, with your eyes open and your breath finding its own pace. Imagine an autumn path beginning just outside an orchard. This is a place made for the journey, not a reconstruction of Keats’s walk. The air is cool near your cheeks, and an apple carries a small weight of water on its skin. Let the first lines arrive as slowly as the fruit has ripened. Behind the sweetness are hands, fields, and the work of harvest. Nothing here has to hurry into winter. As the poem turns toward its smaller sounds, you can leave a little room around each one: a cricket, a bird, the light movement of wings.
poems.alt: Imagined apple orchard in golden morning mist, with red apples and a distant cottage.
poems.imageReading: A moment to look without adding another sentence. Follow the weight of the fruit, then the light in the grass. This original imagined orchard responds to the poem; it does not show Keats’s historical surroundings.
poems.imageFeel: Stay a moment in the orchard’s soft light. You might imagine the rough bark close to your hand, and the small coolness of the apple before it warms against your palm. Then let your attention drift past the fruit to a branch beginning to change color. The world is putting on something bright, and another voice is ready to notice.

poems.title: Autumn
poems.author: Emily Dickinson
poems.poem:
The morns are meeker than they were,
The nuts are getting brown;
The berry's cheek is plumper,
The rose is out of town.

The maple wears a gayer scarf,
The field a scarlet gown.
Lest I should be old-fashioned,
I'll put a trinket on.
poems.edition: Early published text: Poems (1890), “Nature,” XXVIII, editorially titled “Autumn”; reproduced from the collected early-series transcription. This is not the modern Franklin reading text.
poems.history: This eight-line poem appeared as “Autumn” in Dickinson’s first posthumous collection, Poems (1890), edited by Mabel Loomis Todd and T. W. Higginson. The early editors supplied titles and altered aspects of presentation. This orb deliberately preserves that early published text and identifies it, rather than silently combining its title with a modern scholarly transcription.
poems.reading: A season turns into a social occasion. The rose has gone out, the maple wears a scarf, and the field has dressed up. The final gesture is deliciously small: the speaker joins in with a trinket. Nature is neither a distant spectacle nor a solemn teacher; it becomes company.
poems.detail: The poem moves from weather and ripening to clothes and participation. Notice the change from describing “the” world to saying “I’ll.” The last line brings the speaker into the scene with a decision almost anyone could imagine making. That movement gives the little poem its lift.
poems.question: How does the early editorial title “Autumn” shape a reading compared with entering through the first line?
poems.investigation: Compare a scan of the 1890 printing with a manuscript or a documented scholarly apparatus. Keep each version distinct. This is an editorial inquiry, not a claim that Dickinson’s intention can be recovered from one punctuation choice.
poems.feel: The orchard opens into a meadow, and you can let the day become a little lighter. A maple branch holds red against the sky. In the early published Dickinson poem, the landscape dresses itself, and the speaker decides to join it. You need not imagine wearing anything elaborate. Perhaps one leaf is enough: a small brightness carried for the pleasure of its color. Let the smile in those last lines have its own space. The season does not ask you to stand outside and admire it. In this poem, you can belong to the scene.
poems.alt: Scarlet and orange maple leaves against a blue autumn sky and golden meadow.
poems.imageReading: Look at a single leaf before taking in the whole branch. The imagined maple carries Dickinson’s clothing metaphor into color. The scene is newly generated, not an image associated with her manuscript.
poems.imageFeel: Let the red of the leaves meet the blue beyond them. You can look softly, without needing to name every shade. A breeze in the imagined meadow turns one leaf, briefly showing its paler underside. That small motion draws your attention toward water, where sunlight is already moving in little flashes.

poems.title: Merry Autumn
poems.author: Paul Laurence Dunbar
poems.poem:
It’s all a farce,—these tales they tell
     About the breezes sighing,
And moans astir o’er field and dell,
     Because the year is dying.

Such principles are most absurd,—
     I care not who first taught ’em;
There’s nothing known to beast or bird
     To make a solemn autumn.

In solemn times, when grief holds sway
     With countenance distressing,
You’ll note the more of black and gray
     Will then be used in dressing.

Now purple tints are all around;
     The sky is blue and mellow;
And e’en the grasses turn the ground
     From modest green to yellow.

The seed burrs all with laughter crack
     On featherweed and jimson;
And leaves that should be dressed in black
     Are all decked out in crimson.

A butterfly goes winging by;
     A singing bird comes after;
And Nature, all from earth to sky,
     Is bubbling o’er with laughter.

The ripples wimple on the rills,
     Like sparkling little lasses;
The sunlight runs along the hills,
     And laughs among the grasses.

The earth is just so full of fun
     It really can’t contain it;
And streams of mirth so freely run
     The heavens seem to rain it.

Don’t talk to me of solemn days
     In autumn’s time of splendor,
Because the sun shows fewer rays,
     And these grow slant and slender.

Why, it’s the climax of the year,—
     The highest time of living!—
Till naturally its bursting cheer
     Just melts into thanksgiving.
poems.edition: Lyrics of Lowly Life (1896), as presented and identified as public domain by the Academy of American Poets. Ten quatrains.
poems.history: “Merry Autumn” appeared in Lyrics of Lowly Life in 1896. Dunbar was among the first African American poets to gain national recognition. Here he argues directly with a familiar literary habit: treating autumn as a season of mourning. His speaker answers the convention with bright clothes, living creatures, moving water, and the energy of a conversational voice.
poems.reading: Dunbar and Dickinson both dress the landscape, but Dunbar turns color into evidence in an argument. Why, his speaker asks, would a mourning world wear crimson? The argument belongs to a poem. Birds, plants, and streams do not establish a universal emotional meaning for a season. The force is in the freedom to read its brightness differently.
poems.detail: Follow the repeated language of refusal: the opening farce, the absurd principles, the later “Don’t talk to me.” Then hear how the quatrains keep skipping forward. “Wimple” suggests little folds or ripples; “rills” are small streams. The sounds let the water participate in the speaker’s delighted counterargument.
poems.question: When autumn is called sad or merry, what comes from the landscape and what comes from literary expectation?
poems.investigation: Set Dunbar’s clothing images beside Dickinson’s and Keats’s final sounds. Mark the observations separately from the emotions the speakers assign. This is an open interpretive question for this anthology, not an unresolved scientific claim.
poems.feel: At the brook, the light refuses to stay still. You can follow one small gleam as it breaks apart and returns further downstream. Dunbar’s speaker has no patience with the rule that autumn must be sorrowful. Let that refusal be playful rather than another feeling you have to achieve. If your own day is quieter or heavier, the poem can keep its delight without asking you to imitate it. Around the imagined water, crimson leaves move in the current. For a little while, their motion is enough.
poems.alt: A shallow autumn brook reflecting sunlight beneath amber and crimson trees.
poems.imageReading: The little folds of water offer a visual companion to Dunbar’s “ripples.” This is an imagined stream, paired for its movement and reflected color, with no claim that it depicts a place the poet visited.
poems.imageFeel: Let the water carry the eye outward. Each quick brightness belongs to a surface already changing. You can leave the stream exactly as it is and follow the path up the bank, where the trees begin to open. Ahead, a broad blue sky makes room for the whole hillside.

poems.title: October
poems.author: Helen Hunt Jackson
poems.poem:
The month of carnival of all the year,
When Nature lets the wild earth go its way
And spend whole seasons on a single day.
The spring-time holds her white and purple dear;
October, lavish, flaunts them far and near;
The summer charily her reds doth lay
Like jewels on her costliest array;
October, scornful, burns them on a bier.
The winter hoards his pearls of frost in sign
Of kingdom: whiter pearls than winter knew,
Or Empress wore, in Egypt's ancient line,
October, feasting 'neath her dome of blue,
Drinks at a single draught, slow filtered through
Sunshiny air, as in a tingling wine!
poems.edition: “October” from A Calendar of Sonnets. The consulted 1891 printing bears an 1886 copyright date; this is not asserted to be the poem’s first periodical appearance.
poems.history: Jackson’s A Calendar of Sonnets gives each month a fourteen-line poem. The consulted book was printed in 1891 and bears an 1886 copyright date, after her death in 1885. Her October gathers the colors and luxuries of other seasons and spends them extravagantly. The sequence supplies a useful historical frame: autumn appears within a complete annual cycle.
poems.reading: The poem thinks through wealth—jewels, pearls, hoarding, and lavish expenditure. Yet its feast contains a “bier,” a platform associated with a dead body. Splendor and disappearance occupy the same scene. The reference to an Egyptian empress is a poetic comparison, not a documentary account of an identifiable ruler or custom.
poems.detail: The opening eight lines gather spring and summer; the last six turn to winter’s frost and October’s air. Follow the change from owning beautiful things to drinking the day. “Charily” means sparingly or cautiously. October’s extravagance becomes more vivid beside the careful habits assigned to other seasons.
poems.question: Does October’s lavish spending resist loss, celebrate it, or hold both possibilities together?
poems.investigation: Trace the poem’s words for possession and destruction. Compare October with September and November in the same calendar. The collection can test this reading more reliably than a claim about the poet’s private feelings.
poems.feel: You arrive where the hillside opens under blue. The imagined trees carry colors that seem almost too many to keep: amber beside russet, pale gold beside red. Jackson calls October a carnival, but her abundance includes an image of death. You can let both remain. The beauty does not need a promise that it will last, and the ending does not erase the beauty. Let your attention rest on the space between the treetops and the sky. There is no need to gather the whole hillside into memory. One patch of light may be plenty.
poems.alt: Gold and copper autumn trees on a broad hillside beneath a clear blue sky.
poems.imageReading: A wide view after the brook’s close detail. This newly imagined landscape answers the poem’s blue dome and extravagant color; it is a thematic companion rather than a historical location.
poems.imageFeel: Stay with that open blue a little longer. Then imagine the sun lowering until the colors deepen and the spaces between the trees turn cool. A garden wall appears along the path. Beyond it, a small glow gathers the last warmth of the day into a different kind of brightness.

poems.title: Autumn Fires
poems.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
poems.poem:
In the other gardens
  And all up the vale,
From the autumn bonfires
  See the smoke trail!

Pleasant summer over
  And all the summer flowers,
The red fire blazes,
  The grey smoke towers.

Sing a song of seasons!
  Something bright in all!
Flowers in the summer,
  Fires in the fall!
poems.edition: From A Child’s Garden of Verses (first published 1885), using the text of the 1905 illustrated edition. Three quatrains; illustrations from that edition are not reproduced here.
poems.history: A Child’s Garden of Verses was first published in 1885. The consulted transcription follows a 1905 illustrated edition. Stevenson compresses a seasonal landscape into a child-sized lyric: gardens, a valley, the red of fire, and the vertical trail of smoke. The simple refrain offers a bright feature for each season.
poems.reading: The poem’s consolation is concrete. It does not bring the summer flowers back; it discovers a different brightness. The fire and smoke are part of the poem’s historical garden scene. In this orb they remain literary images, not instructions to burn autumn leaves.
poems.detail: The short lines keep the picture clear. In the second stanza the fire “blazes” while smoke “towers”: one word supplies intensity, the other height. The last stanza turns these observations into a song. Read the final two lines aloud if you wish and notice their almost balanced exchange.
poems.question: Is the final cheerfulness simple reassurance, or a practiced way of living with change?
poems.investigation: Compare the poem with other seasonal or retrospective passages in A Child’s Garden of Verses. Separate the childlike speaking voice from claims about any actual child’s experience. Both interpretations can be tested against the language without assuming one hidden biography.
poems.feel: In the imagined garden, the day is turning violet. You can remain comfortably back from the small fire, looking at its red center and the pale line of smoke. Stevenson’s poem lets summer be over and still finds something bright. Perhaps you can receive that as an invitation to notice, without making it a rule about your own life. The warmth belongs to this scene; your own body can stay here, supported where you are. Beyond the wall, the hill grows quiet. A little color remains when the flowers are gone.
poems.alt: A small contained bonfire glows in an imagined rural garden at blue hour, with pale smoke.
poems.imageReading: Red warmth against the violet of evening. This original illustration responds to Stevenson’s color and smoke; it is not a historical photograph or practical burning advice.
poems.imageFeel: Watch the imagined smoke become less distinct as it rises. You do not have to follow it all the way. The garden path continues to a sheltered table, where a basket has been set down. After the moving flame, the stillness of ordinary fruit feels especially gentle.

poems.title: To Autumn
poems.author: William Blake
poems.poem:
O Autumn, laden with fruit, and stained
With the blood of the grape, pass not, but sit
Beneath my shady roof; there thou mayst rest,
And tune thy jolly voice to my fresh pipe,
And all the daughters of the year shall dance!
Sing now the lusty song of fruits and flowers.

"The narrow bud opens her beauties to
The sun, and love runs in her thrilling veins;
Blossoms hang round the brows of Morning, and
Flourish down the bright cheek of modest Eve,
Till clust’ring Summer breaks forth into singing,
And feather’d clouds strew flowers round her head.

"The spirits of the air live on the smells
Of fruit; and Joy, with pinions light, roves round
The gardens, or sits singing in the trees."
Thus sang the jolly Autumn as he sat;
Then rose, girded himself, and o’er the bleak
Hills fled from our sight; but left his golden load.
poems.edition: From Poetical Sketches (1783); text as presented by the Academy of American Poets. Three six-line stanzas. Apostrophe shapes are typographically normalized.
poems.history: Blake’s Poetical Sketches appeared in 1783, decades before Keats’s ode. Here autumn is a visitor invited beneath a roof, asked to sing, and allowed to depart. The route ends with this earlier poem by design: our walking order is thematic, not a chronology of literary history.
poems.reading: This autumn does not stay, even when hospitality makes a place for him. Yet departure is not emptiness: the fruit remains. The supernatural presences belong to Blake’s poetic imagination. Read them as personification and visionary language, not as a description of biological processes or a belief attributed to all people of his period.
poems.detail: The speaker’s invitation occupies the first stanza; Autumn’s song begins in quotation marks and continues into the third. Then the framing voice returns with “Thus sang.” Notice the final turn: the departing figure leaves a tangible load. The poem changes absence into a scene that still has weight and color.
poems.question: What changes when a season becomes a guest, rather than a landscape or a mood?
poems.investigation: Compare Blake’s visitor with Keats’s harvest worker, Dickinson’s dressed landscape, and Dunbar’s laughing world. These are distinct poetic constructions. This orb leaves their differences available for further reading instead of deciding that autumn has one final meaning.
poems.feel: At the table, you find grapes and pears in the evening light. Blake imagines Autumn as a guest who sings and then leaves his harvest behind. You need not picture an actual person passing through. Let the poem’s figure remain a figure, and let the fruit be something your imagination can almost hold. Around it gather the scenes you have crossed: the orchard’s fullness, a bright leaf, the brook’s movement, an open sky, and a little warmth after sunset. None has to become a lesson. For now, you can simply let them share the same quiet table.
poems.alt: Purple grapes and golden pears on a rustic sheltered table overlooking quiet autumn hills.
poems.imageReading: The journey closes with a still life rather than an empty horizon. An original imagined table gives visual weight to Blake’s remaining harvest, without representing an actual scene from his life.
poems.imageFeel: You can leave the basket where it is. There is nothing more to gather before returning. Let the imagined hills grow soft at the edge of your attention, and notice the real surface supporting you. Perhaps feel your feet, or the contact of your hands. Let your eyes find an ordinary color in the room. Autumn has held more than one voice: fullness, play, delight, splendor, warmth, and departure. You can return carrying whichever small detail stayed with you—or simply the ease of having paused.
